questions.q: What does an Inner join output?
options: Every row from the left stream only
Only rows with matching values in both streams
Every row from both streams, matched or not
Only rows that don't match in either stream
questions.explain: Inner join keeps only rows that find a match in both the left and right streams — unmatched rows from either side are dropped.

questions.q: How do you configure a non-equi join (like greater-than instead of equals)?
options: Only Full outer joins can use non-equi conditions
Switch the operator dropdown between the two key columns, and enable Fixed broadcasting on at least one side
Non-equi joins aren't supported in mapping data flows at all
Use a Filter transformation instead of Join
questions.explain: By default a join matches on equality, but changing the operator between columns enables conditions like > or !=, which require Fixed broadcasting on at least one stream.

questions.q: What happens to a column that isn't in an Aggregate transformation's group-by clause or any aggregate expression?
options: It passes through unchanged automatically
It doesn't flow through to the output at all
It causes the data flow to fail
It gets converted to a string type automatically
questions.explain: Aggregate behaves like a SQL SELECT with GROUP BY — any column not explicitly included in the group-by or an aggregate expression simply disappears from the output.

questions.q: How do you keep an extra column around through an Aggregate transformation?
options: Aggregate it explicitly with a function like first() or last(), or rejoin it afterward with a self-join
Rename it using a Select transformation before aggregating
It's impossible to keep any column not in the group-by clause
Switch the Aggregate transformation to a Filter transformation
questions.explain: Wrapping the column in an aggregate function like first() or last() (often via a column pattern) keeps it in the output, one value per group.

options: Deduplication only works on numeric columns
Group by the columns that define a duplicate, apply first()/last()/max()/min() to the rest via a column pattern, and duplicates collapse to one row per group
Deduplication requires the Join transformation, not Aggregate
Aggregate can only count duplicates, never actually remove them
questions.explain: Grouping by the duplicate-defining columns and applying a heuristic aggregate function to everything else collapses each group of duplicates down to a single representative row.
